title: When 10 Days Turns Into 2.5 Months: What Actually Happens When a Critical Part Runs Short
summary: Centralized procurement won’t prevent every upstream issue, but it ensures a dedicated team keeps working when a single buyer runs out of options.
body_markdown:
##


That kind of distributed process is exactly what turns a single missing part into a stalled kitting line, a missed ship date, and a build crew idle while one part number holds up an entire program.


A few months ago, a large order of an easy to find part ran straight into that kind of squeeze. What followed is a more honest picture of what “supply chain infrastructure partner” actually means than any tidy success story could give you.


## The part that wouldn't ship


The part in question? Common components that normally ship in about 10 days but instead got caught in an industry-wide supply crunch. Lead times stretched well past what anyone had quoted.


For a manufacturer running builds across multiple programs, a delay like that doesn't just push out one line item; it threatens the schedule for everything downstream of it. A single buyer working one supplier relationship at a time has limited options once a part is on backorder. The instinct is often to wait and hope the lead time holds. Cofactr's team didn't do that.


## Working every angle at once


Instead of tracking one order down one channel, Cofactr's procurement team worked the problem from several directions at once. instead of staying locked to a single source, the team split the remaining need across multiple distributors and evaluated broker availability as a fallback, checking directly with the customer on whether broker-sourced parts would be acceptable in an urgent situation.


The Cofactr team treated the outcome as their responsibility, not just the order. Instead of waiting for the customer to ask, they proactively connected with the customer to walk through where things stood and what came next.


Around the same time, that persistence on the sourcing side also turned up real supply. Cofactr’s AI-powered platform has direct connections across a wide network of distributors and suppliers, so instead of a buyer manually refreshing individual supplier sites, stock and pricing changes surface automatically, in one place, as they happen. When a shortage hits, the Cofactr platform helps split demand intelligently across multiple sources instead of waiting on one, so a shortfall in one channel doesn't have to stall the whole order. None of that replaces the team, it's what empowers a buyer to act in the moment instead of finding out a week later that a window has already closed. That's the strategic difference.


## Where it landed


What actually closed the gap wasn't any single tactic, it was Cofactr's team treating "find the part" as an active, ongoing search rather than a box to check once.


That kind of proactive sourcing is only possible because of what's powering it. That combination of people and technology is how a Cofactr buyer discovered thousands of the needed part sitting at a distributor in time for the customer to place a large order before the window closed, and how, weeks later, the Cofactr team discovered a supplier offering more units of a related part and moved to secure it before the customer even had to ask.


The remaining volume shipped out over the following weeks, delivered in batches with tracking shared proactively so the customer's receiving team always knew what was coming and when, which meant production kept moving instead of stalling out waiting on a single line item.


The outcome wasn't just fulfilling a hard-to-find part order. It was a customer seeing firsthand what it actually means to have Cofactr in place. "Trusted partner" undersells it. A partner is something you call on when you need help; what showed up here was infrastructure. The always-on layer running underneath sourcing, procurement, and delivery, catching a shortage before it ever reaches the customer's line. That's not a nice-to-have bolted on top of procurement. It’s what electronic component supply chain infrastructure for critical hardware actually means.


## The takeaway


Centralizing procurement doesn't guarantee that nothing ever goes wrong upstream. What it guarantees is a dedicated team that's still working the problem after a single buyer would have run out of options.
